property_summary: For any caller with zero prior tokenBalance, calling airDrop increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that adds 0 breaks this because some caller's tokenBalance does not increase by 20 after airDrop.

After any single successful airDrop call by an address that initially had zero balance and which the supportsToken check accepts, the caller's tokenBalance remains non-decreasing across a subsequent identical airDrop attempt (i.e., the reference allows multiple sequential calls from the same caller while the buggy modifier that never releases the lock can make a later call fail and thus leave balances different).

For any caller address A and any helper attacker address B that claims to support the token, performing two sequential airDrop calls from A (both routed through B as the external msg.sender for supportsToken) always results in tokenBalance(A) being non-decreasing on the correct contract (because the reentrancy lock is released), whereas the mutant that never releases the lock can make the second call revert or fail causing tokenBalance(A) to not increase as expected.

For any addresses caller and helper that claims to support the token, making a single airDrop call from caller (with helper used as msg.sender for supportsToken check) leaves c._locked false afterwards in the correct contract so a subsequent airDrop from a different caller can succeed and increase that different caller's tokenBalance; the mutant that never resets _locked can block later airDrop calls causing tokenBalance for some addresses to differ — we capture this by fuzzing two addresses and checking that after a first successful airDrop by addrA (routed through helper), a second airDrop by addrB also succeeds on the reference, i.e. tokenBalance(addrB) == 20, which the mutant can violate.

For any two distinct callers A and B and any helper that correctly reports support for the token, if A successfully calls airDrop (so A's balance becomes 20), then the contract is not left locked and B can subsequently successfully call airDrop too (so B's balance becomes 20); the mutant that fails to release the lock can prevent B's airDrop and thus break this property.

For any two distinct EOA callers A and B that pass the supportsToken check, after A successfully calls airDrop (so tokenBalance(A) == 20) the contract is not left permanently locked and B can subsequently call airDrop successfully (so tokenBalance(B) == 20); the mutant that never releases the lock leaves _locked true and can make B's airDrop fail, violating this.

For any caller with zero initial tokenBalance, calling airDrop will increase that caller's tokenBalance by 20 in the reference C; the mutant flips the hasNoBalance check so callers with zero balance cannot receive the airdrop, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller address that currently has zero tokenBalance, calling airDrop should succeed and increase that caller's tokenBalance by 20 in the reference; the mutant requiring tokenBalance>0 forbids such calls and thus breaks this property for some callers.

For any caller address that currently has zero tokenBalance, calling airDrop should succeed and after the call that caller's tokenBalance equals 20 (the mutant requires tokenBalance>0 and thus forbids zero-balance callers, so it will break this property for some input).

For any caller address with zero initial tokenBalance, calling airDrop should succeed and set that caller's tokenBalance to 20; the mutant requires tokenBalance>0 and thus prevents zero-balance callers from receiving the airdrop.

For any caller address that currently has a positive tokenBalance, calling airDrop reverts (fails) on the reference because hasNoBalance requires zero balance, but the mutant (which requires balance>0) will allow the call to proceed for such callers — so the reference always prevents airDrops from positive-balance callers while the mutant permits them.

For any caller address with zero prior tokenBalance, calling airDrop always increases their tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that adds 10 will violate this for some caller (fuzzer can find an address with zero balance and observe the final balance != 20).

For any caller with zero prior tokenBalance who is recognized by Bank as supporting the token, calling airDrop always results in their tokenBalance increasing to 20 in the correct contract; the mutant that adds 10 breaks this by leaving the balance at 10 for some inputs.

For any caller address that currently has zero tokenBalance and whose msg.sender (the caller) reports supportsToken() == keccak256("Nu Token"), calling airDrop always leaves their tokenBalance equal to 20 in the reference implementation; the mutant that adds only 10 will leave it at 10 for some fuzzed caller and thus violate this rule.

For every caller, calling airDrop when their tokenBalance is initially zero increases their public tokenBalance to exactly 20 (reference enforces one-per-address); the mutant that removes hasNoBalance allows callers with nonzero initial balance to receive another +20, breaking this one-time-airdrop rule for some inputs.

For any caller address, calling airDrop once when their initial tokenBalance is arbitrary yields tokenBalance == 20 if and only if their initial balance was 0 (the reference enforces that only addresses with zero balance can receive +20; the mutant that removes hasNoBalance allows additional calls to increase balances beyond a single 20 for addresses with nonzero initial balance).

For every caller address, after calling airDrop once from that address, the tokenBalance equals 20 if and only if the caller's initial tokenBalance was 0 — the reference enforces that airDrop only succeeds for addresses with zero balance (one-time airdrop); the mutant (which removes hasNoBalance) allows callers with nonzero initial balance to increase their balance, breaking this one-time property for some inputs.

For every caller address that already has a nonzero tokenBalance prior to calling airDrop, the reference contract will revert (preventing any additional airdrop), whereas the mutant removing the hasNoBalance modifier allows such callers to succeed and increase their balance for some inputs.

For every caller address, if they call airDrop twice in a row (without resetting state), the reference contract ensures the second call always reverts (one-time airdrop), while the mutant that removed hasNoBalance allows the second call to succeed for some addresses.

For every caller, calling airDrop increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 and is non-reentrant (the call cannot re-enter to increase balance further); the mutant breaks this by mis-setting the reentrancy guard allowing a reentrant attacker to receive >20.

For any attacker address, a single airDrop call on the correct contract always increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 (no reentrant extra increments); the buggy mutant mis-sets the reentrancy guard allowing a reentrant attacker to gain more than 20 in some inputs.

For any caller address, a single call to airDrop on the correct contract always leaves that caller's tokenBalance equal to exactly 20 (no reentrant extra increments); the mutant mis-sets the reentrancy guard allowing a reentrant attacker contract to re-enter and obtain a tokenBalance > 20 for some attacker addresses, violating the rule.

For any attacker contract address A that advertises support for the token, a single call to airDrop by A on the correct contract results in tokenBalance[A] being exactly 20 (non-reentrant); the mutant that clears the lock before the call allows a reentrant attacker to cause tokenBalance[A] > 20 for some attacker behavior.

For any caller address that initially has zero token balance and whose supportsToken() returns the correct magic value, a single external airDrop() call on the correct contract either succeeds exactly once and leaves tokenBalance == 20 (no extra state changes via nested external calls); the mutant that clears the lock before the call can allow a malicious callee to re-enter via supportsToken() (called during the modifier) and cause tokenBalance to become >20, violating the invariant.

For any caller address, calling airDrop() on the correct contract always increases that caller's tokenBalance from 0 to 20 (succeeds and sets tokenBalance[msg.sender]==20); the mutant which checks for a different token literal causes the supportsToken check to fail for an honest Bank callee and thus airDrop() will revert (or leave balance 0) for those callers, so there exist caller addresses that the mutant will not credit while the reference always does.
